sections.title: Tokens, not words
paragraphs: {{largeLanguageModel}}s do not read words the way humans do. Before any text enters the {{model}}, it is split into {{token}}s — fragments that can be whole words, parts of words, or punctuation.

Tokenization is deterministic: the same text always yields the same {{token}} sequence. Common words like "the" are single {{token}}s; rare words or code may split across several. This is why {{contextWindow}} limits are measured in {{token}}s, not words or characters.
Once tokenized, each {{token}} becomes a vector of numbers — an {{embedding}}. The {{model}} processes these {{embedding}}s through layers of computation to predict what {{token}} comes next.

Understanding {{token}}s matters because {{prompt}} length, answer length, and cost are all measured in {{token}} counts. A 4,096-{{token}} {{contextWindow}} is roughly 3,000 English words, but that varies by language and domain.
Next: how transformers use {{attention}} to decide which {{token}}s matter most when predicting the next one.
bullets: {{token}} — a fragment of text the {{model}} processes (word, subword, or character).

check.prompt: Your prompt is exactly 100 words. A colleague says: "That is 100 {{token}}s, right?" What is the accurate reply?
check.answer: Probably more than 100 tokens — words can split into multiple tokens
choices: Yes — words and tokens are always one-to-one.
Probably more than 100 tokens — words can split into multiple tokens
Probably fewer than 100 tokens — most words combine.
Impossible to say — tokens are random.
check.explanation: Rare words, code, and punctuation often split into multiple {{token}}s. A 100-word prompt may be 120–150 {{token}}s depending on vocabulary.

sections.title: Attention: which tokens matter
paragraphs: The key idea behind transformers is {{attention}}: when predicting the next {{token}}, the {{model}} weighs which prior {{token}}s are most relevant. If the prompt says "The capital of France is," the {{model}} focuses on "France" and "capital" more than "The" or "is."

{{attention}} is learned during training. The {{model}}'s {{weights}} encode patterns like "subjects and verbs agree," "pronouns refer to recent nouns," and "answer formats follow question wording." At inference the {{model}} applies these patterns to your specific {{prompt}}.

This mechanism is why transformers handle long context better than older architectures. Every {{token}} can attend to every other {{token}} in the {{contextWindow}}, so distant references ("As I said 50 sentences ago...") stay accessible.
Click each example below to see what {{attention}} highlights. Notice how the {{model}} prioritizes task-relevant {{token}}s over filler words.

reveals.prompt: Prompt: "Translate 'hello' to Spanish." — which tokens get high attention?
reveals.reveal: "Translate," "hello," and "Spanish" — the task verb and key nouns. "To" and the quotes are low-weight filler.

reveals.prompt: Prompt: "Summarize the document. Focus on financial metrics." — which tokens matter?
reveals.reveal: "Summarize," "financial," and "metrics" — the instruction and constraint. "The" and "on" are structural glue.

reveals.prompt: Prompt: "Answer yes or no: Is Paris in Germany?" — which tokens guide the answer?
reveals.reveal: "Paris," "Germany," and the question structure. The model attends to geography facts learned during training.

check.prompt: In one short phrase: what is {{attention}} in a transformer {{model}}?
check.answer: Weighing which prior tokens are most relevant
check.explanation: {{attention}} lets the {{model}} prioritize certain {{token}}s over others when predicting the next {{token}}, based on learned patterns.

sections.title: Next-token prediction at scale
paragraphs: Training a {{largeLanguageModel}} is fundamentally a giant {{supervisedLearning}} task: predict the next {{token}} given all prior {{token}}s. The training data is text from books, web pages, code repos — billions of examples where the {{target}} is simply the next word.

The {{model}} starts with random {{weights}}, makes terrible {{prediction}}s, measures error ({{loss}}), and updates {{weights}} to do better. Repeat that trillions of times on trillions of {{token}}s, and the {{model}} learns grammar, facts, reasoning patterns, and even some coding ability.

Once trained, you do not retrain for every new task. You write a {{prompt}} that conditions the {{model}}'s existing knowledge: "Translate this," "Summarize that," "Score this answer." The {{model}} predicts {{token}}s that fit your instruction.
This is why transformers are called "foundation models" — they learn broad patterns once, then adapt to thousands of tasks via prompting or light fine-tuning.
Next: production concerns — cost, latency, and safety when deploying at scale.
bullets: Training: predict next {{token}} on billions of examples.
{{weights}} encode grammar, facts, reasoning from the training corpus.
Inference: condition via {{prompt}}, generate {{token}}s, no retraining.

check.prompt: A {{largeLanguageModel}} was trained to predict next {{token}}s on web text. Can it answer math questions it never saw during training?
check.answer: Yes — if math patterns appeared in the training data, it can generalize to new problems
choices: No — it can only repeat exact training examples.
Yes — if math patterns appeared in the training data, it can generalize to new problems
No — you must fine-tune on math problems first.
Yes — but only if you paste the answer into the prompt.
check.explanation: Transformers learn patterns (e.g., "addition works like this") from diverse examples. They generalize to new instances of those patterns at inference time.
